Title: A Study into Validating a Coupled Method of Characteristics and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo Method Against Empirical Data
Abstract: The following will outline the methodology and results of validating a coupled Method of Characteristics (MOC) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method. This research focused specifically on modeling plume impingement, induced by Reaction Control System (RCS) thrusters that flew on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA’s) space shuttle Discovery. For each simulation, the continuum portion of the RCS thruster was simulated using MOC for solving hyperbolic Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) and computed with the NASA code, Reacting and Multi-phase Program (RAMP). The solution was then implemented as a starting condition into the NASA DSMC code, Direct Simulation and Monte Carlo Analysis Code (DAC). Typically, DSMC models rely on code-to-code validation for fidelity. The significance of this research is in its ability to validate its models against empirical data. Prior to computing solutions for these simulations, the mesh size and structure were optimized and many variants of DSMC input parameters were iterated on in order to acquire a reliable, mesh-independent, fully optimized numerical solution.

Title: New Third-Order Moments for the CBL
Abstract: Turbulent convection is an inherently non-local phenomenon and a primary condition for a successful treatment of the CBL (convective boundary layer) is a reliable model of non-locality. In the dynamic equations governing the convective flux, the turbulent kinetic energy, etc., non-locality is represented by the third-order moments, TOMs. Since the simplest form, the so-called down gradient approximation (DGA), severely underestimates the TOMs (up to an order of magnitude), a more physical model is needed. In 1994, an analytical model was presented which was derived directly from the dynamical equations for the TOMs. It considerably improved the DGA but was a bit cumbersome to use and, more importantly, it was based on the quasi-normal (QN) approximation for the fourth-order moments. Here, we present a new analytic expression for the TOMs which is structurally simpler than the 1994 expression and which avoids the QN approximation. The resulting fit to the LES data is superior to that of the 1994 model.

Abstract: Clay minerals are common in ancient terrains on Mars and their presence at the surface alludes to aqueous processes in the Noachian to Early Hesperian (>3.5 Ga). Abstract: Currently, the major reliability characteristic of tantalum capacitors is the failure rate, which is a constant used to characterize random failures of electronic components. Specifics of physical processes resulting in degradation and failures in polymer and MnO2 tantalum capacitors are discussed, and the increase of IM failures with the level of stress is explained. Title: Statistical Characteristics of Extreme Precipitation Events Over Tropical Oceans and Land Using Five Years of IMERG Data
Abstract: This study provides a statistical analysis of tropical extreme precipitation events (EPEs) using five years (2006-2010) of IMERG V06 Final Run data. EPE life cycles and spatial structures are tracked with a Lagrangian algorithm that allows spatial and temporal gaps and captures both light and heavy/extreme precipitation. Across the tropics, we identify 6.84 million EPEs (~3.99 million oceanic and ~2.85 million land) and examine their frequency and key characteristics, including duration, intensity, rainfall, and areal coverage, over tropical land and oceans. Geographic and seasonal patterns follow major convective regions, such as the ITCZ, with event counts migrating meridionally alongside the seasonal progression of tropical rainfall. Local event counts are dominated by 1–6-h events everywhere, while 6–12-h events make up a higher percentage over land. Diurnal cycles differ sharply: land EPEs peak in the afternoon, whereas oceanic events exhibit weaker morning and late-evening peaks. Substantial land-ocean contrasts also emerge in EPE properties.

Abstract: Cloud microphysics budgets in the tropical deep convective regime are analyzed based on a 2-D cloud resolving simulation. Abstract: As new operational paradigms and additional aircraft are being introduced into the National Airspace System (NAS), maintaining safety in such a rapidly growing environment becomes more challenging. Abstract: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has proposed a concept of operations geared towards achieving increased arrival throughput at U.S. Airports, known as the Simplified Aircraft-based Paired Approach (SAPA) concept. In this study, a preliminary characterization of a wake-free safe zone (WFSZ) for the SAPA concept has been performed. The experiment employed Monte-Carlo simulations of varying approach profiles by aircraft pairs to closely-spaced parallel runways. Three different runway lateral spacings were investigated (750 ft, 1000 ft and 1400 ft), along with no stagger and 1500 ft stagger between runway thresholds. The paired aircraft were flown in a leader/trailer configuration with potential wake encounters detected using a wake detection surface translating with the trailing aircraft. The WFSZ is characterized in terms of the smallest observed initial in-trail distance leading to a wake encounter anywhere along the approach path of the aircraft. The results suggest that the WFSZ can be characterized in terms of two primary altitude regions, in ground-effect (IGE) and out of ground-effect (OGE), with the IGE region being the limiting case with a significantly smaller WFSZ.

Title: Confidence-Based Feature Acquisition
Abstract: Confidence-based Feature Acquisition (CFA) is a novel, supervised learning method for acquiring missing feature values when there is missing data at both training (learning) and test (deployment) time. To train a machine learning classifier, data is encoded with a series of input features describing each item. In some applications, the training data may have missing values for some of the features, which can be acquired at a given cost. A relevant JPL example is that of the Mars rover exploration in which the features are obtained from a variety of different instruments, with different power consumption and integration time costs. The challenge is to decide which features will lead to increased classification performance and are therefore worth acquiring (paying the cost). To solve this problem, CFA, which is made up of two algorithms (CFA-train and CFA-predict), has been designed to greedily minimize total acquisition cost (during training and testing) while aiming for a specific accuracy level (specified as a confidence threshold).

Title: Trade Space Assessment for Human Exploration Mission Design
Abstract: Many human space exploration mission architecture assessments have been performed over the years by diverse organizations and individuals. Direct comparison of metrics among these studies is extremely difficult due to widely varying assumptions involving projected technology readiness, mission goals, acceptable risk criteria, and socio-political environments. However, constant over the years have been the physical laws of celestial dynamics and rocket propulsion systems. A finite diverse yet finite architecture trade space should exist which captures methods of human exploration - particularly of the Moon and Mars - by delineating technical trades and cataloging the physically realizable options of each. A particular architectural approach should then have a traceable path through this "trade tree". It should be pointed out that not every permutation of paths will result in a physically realizable mission approach, but cataloging options that have been examined by past studies should help guide future analysis.

Abstract: The craftsmen in the Roman Empire who constructed the Lycurgus Cup 17 centuries ago probably didn't think their artifact would survive for nearly 2,000 years as a prized possession. And they certainly couldn't have known that the technology they used to make it would eventually become an important part of space exploration. Carved from one solid mass, the cup is one of the few complete glass objects from that period, and the only one made from dichroic glass. Meaning "two-colored" in Greek, dichroic glass was originally created by adding trace amounts of gold and silver to a large volume of glass melt. The resulting medium partially reflects the light passing through it, causing an observer to see different colors depending on the direction of the light source. The Lycurgus Cup, for example, is famous for appearing green in daylight and red when lit at night, symbolic of the ripening grapes used to fill it with wine. Abstract: The black-hole X-ray binary transient GRO J1655-40 underwent an outburst beginning in early 2005. We present the results of our multi-wavelength observational campaign to study the early outburst spectral and temporal evolution, which combines data from X-ray (RXTE, INTEGRAL), radio (VLA) and optical (ROTSE, SMARTS) instruments. During the reported period the source left quiescence and went through four major accreting black hole states: low-hard, hard intermediate, soft intermediate and high-soft. We investigated dipping behavior in the RXTE band and compare our results to the 1996-1997 case, when the source was predominantly in the high-soft state, finding significant differences. We consider the evolution of the low frequency quasi-periodic oscillations and find that the frequency strongly correlates with the spectral characteristics, before shutting off prior to the transition to the high-soft state. We model the broad-band high-energy spectrum in the context of empirical models, as well as more physically motivated thermal and bulk-motion Comptonization and Compton reflection models.

Abstract: Controlling discretization error is a remaining challenge for computational fluid dynamics simulation. To enable application to high O(10(exp 7)) Reynolds number turbulent flows, a hybrid approach is utilized that freezes the near-wall boundary layer grids and adapts the grid away from the no slip boundaries. Abstract: The transition between gravity environments is one of the most complex, high-risk phases of exploration missions. Abstract: While tropical cyclone rainfall has a large axisymmetric component, previous observational and theoretical studies have shown that environmental vertical wind shear leads to an asymmetric component of the vertical motion and precipitation fields. NASA technical report (published 2012)
Title: Development and Applications of a Stage Stacking Procedure
Abstract: The preliminary design of multistage axial compressors in gas turbine engines is typically accomplished with mean-line methods. These methods, which rely on empirical correlations, estimate compressor performance well near the design point, but may become less reliable off-design. For land-based applications of gas turbine engines, off-design performance estimates are becoming increasingly important, as turbine plant operators desire peaking or load-following capabilities and hot-day operability. The current work develops a one-dimensional stage stacking procedure, including a newly defined blockage term, which is used to estimate the off-design performance and operability range of a 13-stage axial compressor used in a power generating gas turbine engine. The new blockage term is defined to give mathematical closure on static pressure, and values of blockage are shown to collapse to curves as a function of stage inlet flow coefficient and corrected shaft speed. In addition to these blockage curves, the stage stacking procedure utilizes stage characteristics of ideal work coefficient and adiabatic efficiency.

Rust RFC pull request (opened 2018-03-27)
Title: rfc: make cargo install extensible
Description: The goal of this RFC is to introduce the ability for an end user to be able to extend the `cargo install` command arbitrarily to include instructions that should be executed occur after `cargo install `. We are in no way suggesting that `cargo install` should be the definitive or exclusive distribution mechanism, or that it should supplant other distribution mechanisms such as platform package management tools; we are only proposing to improve the experience for the class of applications that already depend on cargo as a distribution platform today, notably small CLI applications and development tools for the Rust ecosystem. Additionally, this proposal will make `cargo install` more useful for the larger set of rust applications that leverage the larger, often preferred, platform-specific distribution workflows, which typically want to install into a temporary directory and package the result. This point is discussed further in the “Rationale and Alternatives” section.

Title: RFC: let-else statements
Description: Introduce a new `let PATTERN: TYPE = EXPRESSION else DIVERGING_BLOCK;` construct (informally called a let-else statement), the counterpart of if-let expressions. If the pattern match from the assigned expression succeeds, its bindings are introduced *into the surrounding scope*. If it does not succeed, it must diverge (return `!`, e.g. return or break). Technically speaking, let-else statements are refutable `let` statements. The expression has some restrictions, notably it may not be an `ExpressionWithBlock` or `LazyBooleanExpression`. This RFC is a modernization of a 2015 RFC (pull request 1303) for an almost identical feature. In particular: Josh Triplett, scottmcm, Mario Carneiro, Frank Steffahn, Dirkjan Ochtman, and bstrie.

Rust RFC pull request (opened 2014-09-17)
Title: Allocator RFC, take II
Description: Add a standard allocator interface and support for user-defined allocators, with the following goals: Allow libraries to be generic with respect to the allocator, so that users can supply their own memory allocator and still make use of library types like `Vec` or `HashMap` (assuming that the library types are updated to be parameterized over their allocator). In particular, stateful per-container allocators are supported. Support ability of garbage-collector (GC) to identify roots stored in statically-typed user-allocated objects outside the GC-heap, without sacrificing efficiency for code that does not use `Gc `. Do not require an allocator itself to extract metadata (such as the size of an allocation) from the initial address of the allocated block; instead, force the client to supply size at the deallocation site. In other words, do not provide a `free(ptr)`-based API.

Rust RFC pull request (opened 2014-05-28)
Title: RFC: "as" should be "as PATH" or "as (TYPE)"
Description: Start Date: 2014-05-28. The `as` production in the grammar should be `as PATH` or `as (TYPE)` (with the parentheses). When adding `+` to separate trait object paths from bounds in the type grammar, we broke a bunch of code that looked like `1 as uint + 3`. This is because the type parser is greedy and started parsing after `+`. This will allow us. The `as` production in the grammar should be `as PATH` or `as (TYPE)` (with the parentheses). `PATH` productions in this context should be parsed as types. Complex types with `as` might become slightly more verbose, and the grammar becomes slightly more complicated. The impact of not doing this is that if we extend the type grammar (e.g. with `+`) then we will break existing code. N/A.

event_rules: Events are applied in ascending order of ts; events with the same ts keep their order in the list.
A status event changes the order's status to its value only if that value comes later in the progression placed → packed → shipped → delivered than the current status; otherwise it is rejected.

A cancel event sets the status to "cancelled", but only while the order is in the first or second stage of the progression; otherwise it is rejected. A cancelled order accepts no further status, cancel or move events (they are rejected).
A move event sets the order's warehouse to its value, unless the order is already in the last stage of the progression (then it is rejected).

A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.
A rejected event has no effect at all and does not change the entity.

regras_de_eventos: Os eventos são aplicados em ordem crescente de ts; eventos com o mesmo ts mantêm a ordem da lista.
Um evento status altera o estado do pedido para o seu valor apenas se esse valor vier depois do estado atual na sequência feito → embalado → enviado → entregue; caso contrário é rejeitado.

Um evento cancel define o estado como "cancelado", mas apenas enquanto o pedido estiver na primeira ou segunda etapa da sequência; caso contrário é rejeitado. Um pedido cancelado não aceita mais eventos status, cancel nem move (são rejeitados).
Um evento move define o armazém do pedido como o seu valor, a menos que o pedido já esteja na última etapa da sequência (então é rejeitado).

Um evento void cancela o efeito do evento cujo id está no campo target, como se nunca tivesse ocorrido (os demais eventos são reaplicados sem ele). Um void não pode ser anulado; um void cujo id de destino não está no registro é ignorado.
Um evento rejeitado não tem nenhum efeito e não altera a entidade.

A receive event adds qty units of sku to bin. A pick event removes qty units of sku from bin, but is rejected if the bin holds fewer than qty units of that sku. A move event takes qty units of sku from bin to bin2 and is rejected if bin holds fewer than qty units.
A count event sets the quantity of sku in bin to qty exactly, whatever it was before.

A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.
A rejected event has no effect at all and does not change the entity.

event_rules: Events are applied in ascending order of ts; events with the same ts keep their order in the list.

A status event sets the ticket's status to its value if the ticket is not "merged" or "closed"; for a "closed" ticket it is rejected. Moving to "open" is only accepted from "resolved" (a reopen); every other transition is accepted.
An assign event sets the ticket's assignee to its value, unless the ticket is "closed" or "merged" (rejected).

A merge event (ticket = source, value = target ticket) sets the source to "merged" and its assignee is unchanged; the target ticket takes the smaller (more urgent) priority number of the two. A merge is rejected if the source or the target is "closed" or "merged", or if source and target are the same.

A void event cancels the effect of the event whose id is in its target field, as if that event had never happened (all remaining events are applied again without it). A void can itself not be voided; a void whose target id is not in the log is ignored.
A rejected event has no effect at all and does not change the entity.

quy_tắc_sự_kiện: Các sự kiện được áp dụng theo thứ tự ts tăng dần; các sự kiện có cùng ts giữ nguyên thứ tự trong danh sách.

Sự kiện receive thêm qty đơn vị sku vào bin. Sự kiện pick lấy qty đơn vị sku khỏi bin, nhưng bị từ chối nếu bin chứa ít hơn qty đơn vị sku đó. Sự kiện move chuyển qty đơn vị sku từ bin sang bin2 và bị từ chối nếu bin chứa ít hơn qty đơn vị.
Sự kiện count đặt số lượng sku trong bin chính xác bằng qty, bất kể giá trị trước đó là bao nhiêu.

Sự kiện void hủy hiệu lực của sự kiện có id nằm trong trường target, như thể sự kiện đó chưa từng xảy ra (các sự kiện còn lại được áp dụng lại mà không có nó). Bản thân void không thể bị hủy; void có id đích không có trong nhật ký sẽ bị bỏ qua.
Sự kiện bị từ chối hoàn toàn không có tác dụng và không làm thay đổi đối tượng.

state.policy:
Travel and Expense Policy. This policy governs reimbursement of business-trip expenses for employees. Amounts are in euros.
1. Definitions. A "business trip" is a trip with at least one overnight stay away from the employee's home city that has been approved in advance. A "travel day" is any calendar day from the day of departure to the day of return, both included. "Grade" is the employee's grade from 1 to 4 as shown on the claim. City class A, B or C is assigned to the destination in Annex 1.
2. Hotel. The hotel is reimbursed per night up to the cap for the city class and grade (euros per night): class A: 160 (grades 1-2) / 180 (grades 3-4); class B: 125 (grades 1-2) / 150 (grades 3-4); class C: 95 (grades 1-2) / 110 (grades 3-4). Amounts above the cap are not reimbursed; the cap applies to every night.
3. Meals. Meals are reimbursed as a flat allowance of 40 euros per travel day. On the first and the last travel day the allowance is 50 % of that amount. For each meal that was provided free of charge (for example at a conference), the allowance of that travel day is reduced by 20 % of the full daily amount for breakfast and 30 % for lunch or dinner; the allowance of a day never falls below zero. No receipts are needed for the allowance.
4. Flights. Flights are reimbursed at the economy fare. Business class is reimbursed in full only if the flight lasts more than 5 hours and the employee is grade 3 or higher; otherwise the reimbursement is limited to the economy fare that the claim states for the same flight.
5. Local transport. Public transport and taxis at the destination are reimbursed up to 15 euros per travel day in total. Items of more than 25 euros need an original receipt. Items of up to 25 euros without a receipt are reimbursed only if those items together do not exceed 75 euros; otherwise none of them is reimbursed.
6. Excluded items. Alcoholic drinks, minibar, personal entertainment and leisure, spa and fitness, parking fines and any other fines are never reimbursed, even if they appear on a hotel invoice.
7. Private car. If the employee uses a private car, mileage is reimbursed at 0.30 euros per kilometre. This clause does not apply to taxis or rented cars.
8. Late claims. A claim must be submitted within 30 days after the day of return. If it is submitted later but within 60 days, the total reimbursable amount is reduced by 10 %. After 60 days the claim is rejected.
9. Approval. The approver is determined by the total reimbursable amount after all deductions: up to and including 600 euros the line manager approves; above that and up to and including 1800 euros the department head approves; above 1800 euros the finance director approves. A rejected claim needs no approval.
10. Records. Claims and receipts are kept for ten years. Personal data on receipts is processed under the company data protection notice.
Additional provisions (these do not change the numbered clauses above):
- Spouses and guests. Costs for accompanying persons are never reimbursed, including their share of a shared room or meal.
- Trips abroad. For trips to destinations outside the home country a separate foreign-travel annex applies, with country-specific meal allowances between 55 and 95 euros per day. The annex is not part of this policy and is issued by the finance department.
- Training trips. Travel to external training events is booked through the learning platform. The registration fee is paid centrally and does not appear on the claim.
- Currency. Expenses in other currencies are converted at the rate of the card statement. Cash expenses are converted at the rate published by the finance department on the day of the claim.
Annex 1. City classes: A = capital and financial centres; B = other cities above 250,000 inhabitants; C = all other places.

state.policy:
Travel and Expense Policy. This policy governs reimbursement of business-trip expenses for employees. Amounts are in euros.
1. Definitions. A "business trip" is a trip with at least one overnight stay away from the employee's home city that has been approved in advance. A "travel day" is any calendar day from the day of departure to the day of return, both included. "Grade" is the employee's grade from 1 to 4 as shown on the claim. City class A, B or C is assigned to the destination in Annex 1.
2. Hotel. The hotel is reimbursed per night up to the cap for the city class and grade (euros per night): class A: 160 (grades 1-2) / 175 (grades 3-4); class B: 115 (grades 1-2) / 135 (grades 3-4); class C: 85 (grades 1-2) / 105 (grades 3-4). Amounts above the cap are not reimbursed; the cap applies to every night.
3. Meals. Meals are reimbursed as a flat allowance of 48 euros per travel day. On the first and the last travel day the allowance is 60 % of that amount. For each meal that was provided free of charge (for example at a conference), the allowance of that travel day is reduced by 20 % of the full daily amount for breakfast and 30 % for lunch or dinner; the allowance of a day never falls below zero. No receipts are needed for the allowance.
4. Flights. Flights are reimbursed at the economy fare. Business class is reimbursed in full only if the flight lasts more than 5 hours and the employee is grade 4 or higher; otherwise the reimbursement is limited to the economy fare that the claim states for the same flight.
5. Local transport. Public transport and taxis at the destination are reimbursed up to 20 euros per travel day in total. Items of more than 15 euros need an original receipt. Items of up to 15 euros without a receipt are reimbursed only if those items together do not exceed 45 euros; otherwise none of them is reimbursed.
6. Excluded items. Alcoholic drinks, minibar, personal entertainment and leisure, spa and fitness, parking fines and any other fines are never reimbursed, even if they appear on a hotel invoice.
7. Private car. If the employee uses a private car, mileage is reimbursed at 0.30 euros per kilometre. This clause does not apply to taxis or rented cars.
8. Late claims. A claim must be submitted within 45 days after the day of return. If it is submitted later but within 90 days, the total reimbursable amount is reduced by 10 %. After 90 days the claim is rejected.
9. Approval. The approver is determined by the total reimbursable amount after all deductions: up to and including 600 euros the line manager approves; above that and up to and including 2400 euros the department head approves; above 2400 euros the finance director approves. A rejected claim needs no approval.
10. Records. Claims and receipts are kept for ten years. Personal data on receipts is processed under the company data protection notice.
Additional provisions (these do not change the numbered clauses above):
- Training trips. Travel to external training events is booked through the learning platform. The registration fee is paid centrally and does not appear on the claim.
- Booking. Flights and hotels are booked through the travel desk; bookings outside the travel desk are allowed only when the desk cannot offer a comparable option.
- Spouses and guests. Costs for accompanying persons are never reimbursed, including their share of a shared room or meal.
- Currency. Expenses in other currencies are converted at the rate of the card statement. Cash expenses are converted at the rate published by the finance department on the day of the claim.
Annex 1. City classes: A = capital and financial centres; B = other cities above 250,000 inhabitants; C = all other places.

semántica: Los eventos se procesan estrictamente en el orden indicado. Tras un evento, las reglas que coinciden se activan en orden ascendente de número de regla y cada acción se aplica de inmediato.
Una regla con condición solo se activa si la condición se cumple en ese momento; una regla marcada como «única» solo se activa la primera vez que coinciden su disparador y su condición.

Una orden directa del usuario fija el dispositivo y lo pone en retención manual. Las acciones de automatización sobre un dispositivo retenido se omiten hasta el siguiente evento de «modo», que libera todas las retenciones antes de que se activen sus reglas. Las órdenes no activan reglas por sí mismas.
Una cerradura no puede ponerse en «locked» mientras el sensor de su puerta indique «open»: la acción se ignora (la cerradura conserva su valor y no hay cambio). Desbloquear siempre es posible.
Las consignas del termostato (dispositivos heat) se limitan al rango 17-25: un valor mayor o menor se guarda como el límite más cercano.

Cuando un dispositivo cambia realmente de valor (causado por una orden del usuario o por una regla; no hay cambio si ya tenía ese valor), las reglas con disparador «el dispositivo pasa a valor» se ponen en cola y se activan después de las reglas propias del evento actual, en el orden en que ocurrieron los cambios.
Códigos de valor: on@N = luz encendida con N % de brillo, off, on/off para enchufes, locked/unlocked, open/closed para persianas, un número = consigna del termostato en °C.

Una cerradura no puede ponerse en «locked» mientras el sensor de su puerta indique «open»: la acción se ignora (la cerradura conserva su valor y no hay cambio). Desbloquear siempre es posible.
Las consignas del termostato (dispositivos heat) se limitan al rango 17-24: un valor mayor o menor se guarda como el límite más cercano.

Cuando un dispositivo cambia realmente de valor (causado por una orden del usuario o por una regla; no hay cambio si ya tenía ese valor), las reglas con disparador «el dispositivo pasa a valor» se ponen en cola y se activan después de las reglas propias del evento actual, en el orden en que ocurrieron los cambios.
Códigos de valor: on@N = luz encendida con N % de brillo, off, on/off para enchufes, locked/unlocked, open/closed para persianas, un número = consigna del termostato en °C.

questions.instructions: Tras todos los eventos, ¿qué valor tiene meetroom_chiller?

automation_rules: Rule 1: when door_loading becomes unlocked and the current mode is audit: set ups_chiller=20
Rule 2: when the mode becomes lockdown: set loading_shutter=open, noc_psu=on, door_loading=locked, cooling_chiller=28
Rule 3: when motion is detected in noc: set noc_lamp=on@50, loading_shutter=open
Rule 4: when motion is detected in ups and the current mode is not visitor: set ups_lamp=on@100, loading_shutter=closed
Rule 5: when the mode becomes visitor: set loading_psu=off, meetroom_chiller=18, noc_lamp=on@30
Rule 6: when door_loading becomes closed and the current mode is eco: set loading_psu=off, ups_lamp=off
Rule 7 (once): when the clock reaches 23:30: set ups_chiller=24, door_meetroom=unlocked
events_in_order: 5. user command: set ups_lamp to off
semantics: Events are processed strictly in the listed order. After an event, the rules that match it fire in ascending rule number, and each action is applied immediately.
A rule with a condition fires only if the condition holds at that moment; a rule marked "once" fires only the first time its trigger and condition match.

A direct user command sets the device and puts it on manual hold. Automation actions on a held device are skipped until the next "mode" event, which releases all holds before its rules fire. Commands do not trigger rules by themselves.
A lock cannot be set to locked while its door sensor reads open: the action is ignored (the lock keeps its value, and no change happens). Unlocking is always possible.
Thermostat setpoints (heat devices) are limited to the range 18-26: a larger or smaller value is stored as the nearest limit.

When a device actually changes value (caused by a user command or by a rule; no change if it already had that value), rules with trigger "device becomes value" are queued and fire after the current event's own rules, in the order the changes happened.
Value codes: on@N = light on at N % brightness, off, on/off for plugs, locked/unlocked, open/closed for blinds, a number = thermostat setpoint in °C.

state.policy_document: 1. Scope. This policy covers policyholders of Wagtail Mutual for the following categories. Cover starts on 8 January 2026 and runs for one policy year. 2. Categories. (a) Veterinary treatment: Consultations, diagnostics and surgery. Cover 80% of the eligible amount; at most 800 GBP per invoice line counts; annual limit 4000 GBP. (b) Medication: Prescribed drugs. Cover 70% of the eligible amount; at most 150 GBP per invoice line counts; annual limit 600 GBP. (c) Dental: Dental treatment after illness or injury. Cover 60% of the eligible amount; at most 300 GBP per invoice line counts; annual limit 500 GBP; items dated fewer than 30 days after cover starts are not covered. (d) Routine care: Vaccinations and flea treatment. Cover 50% of the eligible amount; at most 80 GBP per invoice line counts; annual limit 150 GBP. 3. Exclusions. Never covered: grooming, boarding, pre-existing conditions. An item that falls under an exclusion is removed before any other step. 4. Calculation order. Step 1: Remove excluded items, items that fall within a waiting period, and items dated more than 120 days before the claim date. Step 2: Cap each remaining item at its per-item amount (per invoice line), then add up the items of each category. Step 3: Apply the cover percentage of the category to its total. Step 4: Reduce each category by the part of its annual limit already used (see the ledger); a category cannot pay more than its remaining limit. Step 5: Add up the categories and, if the deductible has not yet been used this policy year, subtract the deductible of 75 GBP once from the total (never below zero). Step 6: Round the final amount to the nearest cent (half up). 5. Approval. Payouts up to 250 GBP are approved by the claims handler; above 250 and up to 1000 GBP by the senior claims handler; above 1000 GBP by the claims manager. If nothing is eligible the claim is rejected. 6. Valuation. All amounts in the claim are final invoice amounts including taxes; no further tax adjustments apply.

state.rules: Accounting Simplification Order, Article 3: In a given financial year a company passes the size test if it stays at or below at least two of these three limits: turnover 0.9 EUR m; balance sheet total 0.45 EUR m; employees 10 employees. Article 4: A company's status as a micro-entity for a financial year is the same as its status in the previous financial year, unless in each of the two financial years before that year the result of the size test pointed the other way (passed while the previous status was 'not a micro-entity', or failed while it was 'micro-entity'); in that case the status flips. Where fewer than two earlier financial years are on record, the status does not change. Article 5: A micro-entity may use the simplified bookkeeping regime; any other company must use the standard bookkeeping regime.

sources: The Civil Code (code): The minimum notice period for dismissal by the employer is 38 days. This provision is mandatory. In force from 26 April 2026.
The Employment Ordinance (ordinance): The minimum notice period for dismissal by the employer is 33 days. This provision is not mandatory. In force from 20 July 2025.
The Works Agreement (works agreement): The minimum notice period for dismissal by the employer is 20 days. This provision is not mandatory. In force from 22 December 2020.
The Staff Rules (staff rules): The minimum notice period for dismissal by the employer is 44 days. This provision is not mandatory. In force from 5 December 2019.
The offer letter (contract): The minimum notice period for dismissal by the employer is 88 days. This provision is mandatory. In force from 30 November 2019 until 1 March 2026.
ranking_rules: Ranking, highest first: the Civil Code, the Employment Ordinance, the Works Agreement, the Staff Rules, the offer letter.

A provision that is not in force on the relevant date is ignored. Among provisions in force, a provision of a lower-ranking source overrides the provisions of all higher-ranking sources on the same matter, except that no source may fall below the highest figure set by a mandatory provision of any higher-ranking source (the floor).
Statements by managers or in emails are not sources.

routing_policy.organisation: Community Kitchen training helpdesk
routing_rules: Apply the numbered rules in order; the first rule that matches decides the queue.
1. a ticket from region EU (the EU/EEA member states only; the UK is not EU) that contains a personal-data request (access, deletion, export) goes to Training Community Kit Data.
2. a ticket on a plan with an SLA (Business or Enterprise) that has fewer than 4 hours left on its SLA clock goes to Training Community Kit General.
3. a ticket that has been reopened 2 or more times goes to Training Community Kit General.
4. a ticket from a customer on the Enterprise plan goes to Training Community Kit Accounts.

5. Otherwise route by issue type. def 最大公约(a, b):
    步 = 0
    while b:
        a, b = b, a % b
        步 += 1
    return a, 步

def 最小公倍(a, b):
    g, _ = 最大公约(a, b)
    return a // g * b if g else 0

state.problem: We want the latest login per user from a table with millions of rows. A colleague proposes filtering in the same query with WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY ts DESC) = 1. The database throws a syntax error. How should the query be structured?
documents: D1. Sorting With Missing Values: Where NULLs appear in an ORDER BY depends on the system: some treat NULL as larger than any value, so it sorts last in ascending order, others as smaller. NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST make the placement explicit. The same choice affects how LAG, FIRST_VALUE and top-N queries behave.

D2. Looking at Neighbouring Rows: LAG(expr, n, default) returns the value from n rows before the current row in the window order, and LEAD looks forward. The first row of a partition has no predecessor, so LAG returns NULL there unless a default is supplied. They avoid a self-join when computing differences between consecutive rows.

D3. Rounding in Division: In many databases dividing two integer columns performs integer division, so 7 / 2 returns 3. Cast one operand to a decimal or multiply by 1.0 first. The rounding mode of ROUND on exact halves also differs: some systems round half away from zero while others round half to even.

D4. NOT IN With Subqueries: x NOT IN (subquery) is evaluated as a chain of <> comparisons joined by AND. If the subquery returns even one NULL, the result for every x is UNKNOWN or false, so the query returns no rows. NOT EXISTS with a correlated condition, or filtering the subquery with WHERE col IS NOT NULL, avoids the surprise.

D5. Comparisons With Unknown Values: In SQL, comparing anything with NULL using = or <> yields UNKNOWN, not true or false. A WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is true, so rows with unknown results disappear. Use IS NULL, IS NOT NULL or IS DISTINCT FROM to test for missing values explicitly. This also means that a row with a NULL does not satisfy either col = 1 or col <> 1.

D6. Default Frame for Running Totals: A window with ORDER BY and no frame clause uses RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. With RANGE, rows that tie on the ordering key are peers and are all included together, so a running SUM jumps by the whole group of tied rows at once. Specifying ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW counts physical rows one by one.

D7. Join Types and Unmatched Rows: An INNER JOIN keeps only pairs that satisfy the condition. A LEFT JOIN additionally keeps every left row, filling right columns with NULL when no match exists. Placing a condition on a right-table column in the WHERE clause turns the LEFT JOIN back into an inner join because NULL rows are filtered out; put the condition in the ON clause instead to keep unmatched left rows.

D8. Deduplicating With DISTINCT ON and GROUP BY: SELECT DISTINCT removes rows that are identical in all selected columns. To keep one full row per key, PostgreSQL offers DISTINCT ON (key) with an ORDER BY that picks which row survives; in other systems use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by the key. GROUP BY with non-aggregated extra columns is rejected by standard SQL.

D9. Filtering on Window Results: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so their results cannot be referenced in those clauses. To keep only the first row per group, compute ROW_NUMBER() in a subquery or common table expression and filter on it in the outer query. Some dialects offer QUALIFY to filter directly.

D10. Aggregates and Missing Values: Aggregate functions such as SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX ignore NULL inputs. COUNT(column) counts non-null values while COUNT(*) counts rows. AVG over a column with NULLs divides by the number of non-null values, not the number of rows. If the group has only NULLs, SUM and AVG return NULL rather than 0; wrap with COALESCE when a zero is wanted.

D11. Conditional Aggregation: To compute several counts in one pass, use aggregate functions over CASE expressions, for example SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'failed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END). The FILTER clause (FILTER (WHERE status = 'failed')) does the same in dialects that support it. It avoids multiple scans or self-joins.

D12. Numbering Rows: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK: ROW_NUMBER assigns unique consecutive numbers even for ties, in an order that is arbitrary among ties unless the ORDER BY is made unique. RANK gives tied rows the same number and then skips ahead. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number and does not skip. Choose according to whether gaps and ties matter.

state.story:
Ticket ID: TB-4187. The first call reached the telecom billing helpdesk while the night shift was still sorting disputed roaming charges. A supervisor had been found unconscious in the locked storeroom, and the company’s sealed backup handset was missing from its charging cradle. The handset held a test account used to verify billing adjustments, so the incident had already become more than an ordinary workplace assault. Detective Vale arrived as staff were being asked to stay put and keep their hands off the terminals.

The storeroom door had not been forced. Its key opened the room, and the access log showed no useful entry because the lock was old and did not record openings. Vale asked each employee where they had been during the critical half hour. The victim was alive when last seen heading toward the storeroom; later, a cleaner found them on the floor. The medic said the injury was serious, but the victim could not yet give a statement. No one could say whether the missing handset had been the reason for the attack or merely an opportunity that presented itself.

Greta Vogel gave a brisk account while keeping one eye on the ringing helpdesk line. A stockroom register confirmed that she had a key to the locked storeroom where the handset was kept. A colleague had seen Greta by herself near the scene during the critical half hour. When Vale asked what she might gain if the victim were absent, Greta said nothing, and the billing manager’s records backed that up: the victim’s absence brought Greta no advantage. Her name appeared on a separate complaint about a customer’s disputed charge, but the complaint had been resolved and did not connect her to the storeroom.

Owen Pritchard’s reason for resenting the victim was less obscure. The victim’s share of the business was due to pass to Owen, according to a document the company’s solicitor had verified. Yet the access administrator showed Vale a deactivation receipt: Owen had returned their entry code a week earlier. A building guard also remembered Owen leaving before the critical half hour began. Owen claimed he had gone home to settle an argument over an unpaid phone bill, a detail that sounded dramatic but led nowhere; the account belonged to a relative and had no bearing on the missing handset.

Priya Raman had her own grievance. She had been passed over for promotion, and the position had gone to the victim. The decision appeared in the staffing file, along with Priya’s written appeal. Still, the access administrator’s record showed that Priya, like Owen, had turned in her code a week earlier. That did not place her beyond the building: two helpdesk agents saw her alone near the storeroom during the critical half hour. Priya said she had been looking for a dropped headset. A headset was later found beneath a desk in the billing bay, but nothing established that it belonged to her, and the discovery did not explain the attack.

Henrik Dahl had arrived to press the victim about money. A ledger and a series of unanswered messages showed that the victim owed him a large sum. Henrik also had a key to the locked storeroom where the handset had been kept; the facilities clerk recognized the key on his ring and confirmed it still worked. Vale checked who might account for Henrik during the critical half hour. No one could vouch for his whereabouts then. Henrik said he had been walking between the service corridor and the loading area, but the corridor camera was out of order and the loading door showed no reliable record of who passed through.

Vale returned to the helpdesk floor. The agents were still taking calls, their voices lowered as they explained billing holds to customers who had no idea a crime scene sat behind the office doors. The incident log, access paperwork, staffing records, and witness accounts did not all point in the same direction. Some details were motives without a route into the locked room; other details placed people nearby without granting them access or a personal stake. Vale set the statements beside the storeroom key register and waited for the medic to report whether the victim could speak.

You are the investigator who must make the next call: which suspect should be identified as the culprit, based on the evidence?

state.story:
• Interner Vorfall im Abrechnungsteam
• Ermittlungsnotiz der Helpdesk-Leitung

Als die Frühschicht im Telekommunikations-Helpdesk eintraf, lag die zuständige Abrechnungsfachkraft verletzt im schmalen Verbindungsgang hinter dem Büroraum. Sie war bei Bewusstsein, konnte jedoch zunächst nur stockend sprechen. Der Rettungsdienst brachte sie zur Untersuchung fort. Der Gang führte auch zum verschlossenen Lagerraum, in dem ein Spezialwerkzeug aufbewahrt wurde. Die Polizei bat die interne Ermittlerin, Zugangsprotokolle und Aussagen zu sichern, bevor der Betrieb den Bereich wieder freigab.

Der Vorfall hatte sich während einer kritischen halben Stunde ereignet. Die Ermittlerin ließ deshalb für diesen Zeitraum die Gebäudezugänge, die Überwachung und die Arbeitsabläufe prüfen. Ein beschädigtes Gehäuse lag neben der verletzten Fachkraft; die Spuren deuteten darauf hin, dass das Werkzeug aus dem Lagerraum benutzt worden war. Ob der Angriff geplant gewesen war oder aus einer Auseinandersetzung heraus geschah, ließ sich am Fundort nicht erkennen. Auch ein offener Abrechnungsfall, über den im Team gestritten worden war, erwies sich zunächst als wenig aussagekräftig: Mehrere Personen hatten daran gearbeitet.

Tomás Navarro wurde befragt, weil er am Vortag den einzigen Generalschlüsselcode ausgeliehen hatte. Die Ausgabe war im internen Register vermerkt, und Tomás bestätigte die Entleihung. Auf die Frage nach seinem Verhältnis zur verletzten Fachkraft erklärte er, zwischen ihnen habe es keinen Streit gegeben. Die Prüfung der Kamerabilder ergab zudem, dass Tomás während der gesamten kritischen halben Stunde an einem anderen Standort zu sehen war. Die Aufnahmen ließen keine Unterbrechung erkennen, in der er hätte zum Helpdesk gelangen können.

Owen Pritchard kannte sich mit dem Spezialwerkzeug aus. In seiner Aussage erklärte er, im Umgang damit geschult worden zu sein; eine Kollegin bestätigte, dass er regelmäßig bei technischen Arbeiten half. Zugleich schilderten mehrere Beschäftigte sein Verhältnis zur verletzten Fachkraft als ausgesprochen gut. Owen hatte ihr Geld geliehen, als sie vor kurzem Schwierigkeiten gehabt hatte. Für den fraglichen Zeitraum fand die Ermittlerin jedoch niemanden, der bestätigen konnte, wo Owen gewesen war. Er sagte, er habe sich im Gebäude bewegt und niemandem Rechenschaft über jeden seiner Schritte abgelegt. Eine Kamera erfasste ihn dort nicht eindeutig.

Aiko Tanaka hatte Zugang zum Lagerraum, denn sie besaß einen Schlüssel zu dessen Tür. Die Ermittlerin stellte fest, dass der Schlüssel zu den ausgegebenen Berechtigungen gehörte; ein gewaltsames Öffnen der Tür war nicht erforderlich gewesen. Im Gespräch erinnerte Aiko daran, dass die verletzte Fachkraft sie im vergangenen Monat vor anderen Beschäftigten bloßgestellt hatte. Sie beschrieb den Vorfall als demütigend und sagte, sie habe sich danach aus den Gesprächen im Team zurückgezogen. Das Zugangsprotokoll zeigte, dass Aiko wenige Minuten vor dem Vorfall im Gebäude ein- und erst nach dem Vorfall wieder ausgetragen worden war.

Auch Lucía Ferreira hatte am Vortag den einzigen Generalschlüsselcode ausgeliehen. Das Register führte ihre Entleihung ebenso auf wie die von Tomás. Lucía bestritt, mit der verletzten Fachkraft zerstritten zu sein. Nach den Aussagen der Teammitglieder waren beide vielmehr gut miteinander ausgekommen; Lucía hatte der Fachkraft Geld geliehen. Ihr Zugangsausweis wurde wenige Minuten vor dem Vorfall am Gebäude registriert, und der Ausgangseintrag erfolgte erst danach. Lucía sagte, sie habe sich währenddessen im Arbeitsbereich aufgehalten, konnte aber keine Person nennen, die ihren Weg durch das Gebäude beobachtet hatte.

Die Ermittlerin prüfte außerdem zwei Ablenkungen. Ein fehlendes Ladegerät tauchte noch während der Befragungen in einer Schublade auf; es hatte keinen Bezug zum Angriff. Ebenso meldete ein Beschäftigter einen verdächtigen Anruf, doch die Verbindung stammte aus einer automatischen Kundenabfrage und führte zu keinem der Befragten. Die Polizei sicherte das Werkzeug und nahm die Aussagen auf. Für die interne Entscheidung blieben damit die persönlichen Beziehungen, die verfügbaren Zugänge und die belegbaren Aufenthaltsorte im fraglichen Zeitraum maßgeblich. Die Ermittlerin legte ihre Unterlagen der Helpdesk-Leitung vor, ohne die Schlussfolgerung in den Vermerk aufzunehmen.

questions.instructions: Wer hat die verletzte Fachkraft angegriffen?

Dear Mara,

The helpdesk had gone quiet by the time I reached the billing floor. In the locked storeroom, beside the shelves of archived equipment, I found the victim injured and barely conscious. A metal tool lay on the floor nearby. The victim was taken for treatment, and the building was secured while I began asking how someone had reached the room and why.

The room held a portable archive drive containing records used to settle disputed customer bills. Staff said it had been kept there because the records were confidential. The storeroom door showed no sign of damage. The helpdesk supervisor explained that entry could be gained with a physical key; the master code was used for a separate security control. The tool on the floor was normally stored in the room. Its handling required training, though no one could tell me from the scene alone who had used it.

Kofi Mensah spoke with me in the small interview room. He had been publicly humiliated by the victim last month, an argument that several colleagues had witnessed and that was still discussed in the office. Kofi did not deny the dispute. He said the victim had made him look incompetent in front of the team. The storeroom register showed that Kofi had a key to the locked room where the archive drive was kept. A clerk recalled seeing him alone near the scene during the critical half hour. Kofi said he had been looking for a misplaced headset, but no one could confirm that explanation.

Ingrid Solberg had also clashed with the victim. Witnesses described how the victim had publicly humiliated her last month, after a disagreement over a billing procedure. Ingrid had been trained in handling the tool found beside the victim, according to the equipment training record. She told me she knew how to use it safely and had no reason to enter the storeroom. The building’s departure record supported her account on one important point: she had already left before the critical half hour began. A colleague also mentioned that Ingrid had recently complained about a faulty desk lamp, but the complaint had no apparent connection to the incident.

Owen Pritchard was waiting near the helpdesk entrance when I spoke to him. He said he resented being passed over for promotion in favour of the victim. The victim had received the position Owen wanted, and Owen had not hidden his disappointment. The security log also showed that Owen had borrowed the only master code the day before. He insisted he had used it for an approved systems check. Video from another site placed him there throughout the critical half hour. A routine billing alert had appeared under Owen’s account earlier, but the technician who reviewed it found nothing to link it to the injury or the archive drive.

Aiko Tanaka arrived after I had reviewed the entry records. She told me she had discovered that the victim was leaking their secrets, and that the disclosure had destroyed her trust. The visitor register showed that Aiko had signed in at the building a few minutes before the incident and had left after it. Yet the storeroom access list and the key register showed she had no access to the storeroom and no key. She had waited in the public reception area while on the premises, according to the receptionist. Aiko carried a folder of billing notes, but they concerned ordinary account work and did not contain anything from the archive drive.

I checked the records again, then returned to the storeroom. The door, the logs, the staff accounts, and the footage each answered a different question, and none could be set aside simply because another detail sounded more dramatic. The victim remained unable to give a statement. I left the file open for review, with the four accounts and the access evidence arranged in sequence.

state.story:
I am Inspector Mara Venn, and I am recording how a routine billing inquiry became a serious assault investigation at the telecom helpdesk. The victim, the helpdesk’s senior reconciliation clerk, was found injured beside a locked storeroom after a dispute over a sealed backup drive used to preserve billing records. The drive had been kept in that storeroom. The clerk survived, but was too badly hurt to give a reliable account of what happened. A heavy service tool lay nearby; the marks on the storeroom door and the clerk’s injuries made clear that the encounter had not been accidental.

The helpdesk remained open while I took statements and reviewed access records. None of the people I questioned disputed that the victim had been working in the billing area before the assault. The room was busy, and several employees had reasons to be concerned about the victim’s influence over their work. I asked each person separately what had happened between them and the clerk, what access they could obtain, and where they had been during the incident.

Dana Whitlock spoke with measured composure. She acknowledged that the victim had received the promotion Dana wanted, a decision that had left her passed over in favour of the clerk. The access register and a supervisor’s account confirmed that Dana possessed a key for the locked storeroom in which the backup drive was kept. But when the assault occurred, Dana was delivering a presentation to a room of colleagues. Those colleagues independently recalled her speaking throughout the relevant period, and the presentation record supported their account.

Lucía Ferreira’s statement was less controlled. She had found out that the victim was disclosing secrets about her, and she said the discovery had damaged her trust in the clerk. The access log showed that Lucía had checked out the only master code on the day before the assault. That code could open the storeroom’s electronic lock. Yet the building’s camera system placed Lucía at another site for the whole of the critical half hour. The recording was continuous, and the site’s staff confirmed that the person on screen was Lucía.

Owen Pritchard had his own grievance. In his account, he described being publicly humiliated by the victim last month, an episode colleagues remembered as a sharp exchange in the billing area. His training file also showed that he was qualified to handle the service tool found beside the clerk. The sign-in record placed Owen at the building a few minutes before the assault, and the exit record showed that he left after it. A receptionist recalled seeing him inside during the interval. Owen said he had been there on ordinary work, but no record placed him elsewhere during the incident.

Tomás Navarro denied having any dispute with the victim. Several colleagues said the clerk had recently praised Tomás’s work, and no one I interviewed recalled a quarrel between them. The access log also showed that Tomás had borrowed the only master code on the day before the assault. His whereabouts, however, were accounted for: at the time the clerk was attacked, Tomás was giving a presentation to a room of colleagues. The presentation continued without a break, according to those present and the meeting record.

There were distractions in the office. An employee mentioned a billing complaint that had angered the victim, but it concerned a customer who had no access to the storeroom. Another pointed to a disagreement over a misplaced headset; the headset was later found at a desk, and the quarrel had no connection to the assault. Neither lead altered the access records, the witness accounts, or the camera evidence.

I checked the statements against the entry logs, the camera footage, the presentation records, and the storeroom’s access history. The resulting account is consistent about the injury, the secured room, and the people whose actions or circumstances matter. I am sending you the file now, while the records are still available for review.

state.contexte: « Gardons à l’esprit que les clients ne choisissent pas cette infusion au hasard », note la responsable des études, dans ce mémo interne de la boutique de thé en ligne. Une observation a réparti les clients selon la gravité de leurs symptômes et la prise du Mélange Calme. Dans le groupe aux symptômes légers, 112 clients en ont pris et 64 se sont rétablis ; parmi les 247 qui n’en ont pas pris, 174 se sont rétablis. Dans le groupe aux symptômes graves, 46 en ont pris et 19 se sont rétablis ; parmi les 268 qui n’en ont pas pris, 92 se sont rétablis. La gravité influence à la fois la prise de l’infusion et le rétablissement, mais l’infusion ne modifie pas la gravité. Pour l’ajustement, pondérer chaque groupe selon sa part de l’ensemble des clients de l’étude. Ces données observationnelles ne suffisent pas, à elles seules, à établir une causalité.

questions.instructions: Collègue chargé de l’analyse, peux-tu confirmer qu’après cet ajustement selon la gravité, le Mélange Calme augmente le taux de rétablissement ?

state.request:
• PARKS DEPARTMENT — ORDER SHEET NOTES
The delivery record shows 29 crates, with 34 items in each. Once they have arrived, half of the items then in stock are lost. Staff later identify 39 damaged items and discard them; after that, they identify another 62 damaged items and discard those too. The department then increases the remaining stock by half of the amount on hand. Analyst: Please work through these changes in order and put the final result by itself on the last line.
state.response:
First, the crates add 29 × 34 = 986 items.
Losing 50% of the stock at that point leaves 986 × 0.5 = 493 items.
Discarding the 39 damaged items leaves 493 − 39 = 454.
Discarding the additional 62 damaged items leaves 454 − 62 = 392.
The 50% top-up is 392 × 0.5 = 196 items, so the stock becomes 392 + 196 = 588.
588

Rows copied into the analyst’s worksheet, in a hurry:

Request row: A nursery line turns out 67 tree seedlings per hour and operates for 5 hours. After production, add stock equal to 60% of the quantity currently on hand. Divide the resulting stock evenly among 4 planting teams. Show the calculation steps, and make the final line contain nothing but the final figure.

Hourly output × operating time: 67 × 5 = 335 seedlings.
Top-up: 335 × 60% = 201 seedlings.
Stock after top-up: 335 + 201 = 536 seedlings.
Allocation per team: 536 ÷ 4 = 134 seedlings.
Final answer:
134

Строка запроса: Питомническая линия выпускает 67 саженцев деревьев в час и работает 5 часов. После производства добавьте запас, равный 60% имеющегося в данный момент количества. Распределение на бригаду: 536 ÷ 4 = 28 саженцев.

134

api_catalog: calculate_trip_fare: Calculate the total fare for a trip given origin, destination, mode, and time. Accounts for zone crossings, peak/off-peak rates, and route distance.
calibrate_sensor: Triggers an immediate calibration cycle for a specific sensor. This takes 5-10 minutes and will temporarily set the sensor status to 'maintenance'. Irreversible action once started.
check_leave_balance: Retrieves the current remaining leave days for a specified employee and leave type. No side effects; read-only query.
delete_sensor_device: Permanently removes a sensor device from the monitoring network and its historical data. This action cannot be undone. A confirmation prompt is shown before execution.
get_current_aqi_by_sensor: Retrieves the current Air Quality Index (AQI) reading from a specific sensor unit. Data is live from the sensor; readings older than 10 minutes are considered stale.

get_historical_pollutant_trend: Returns time-series data for a single pollutant from a sensor over a 24-hour period. This is used for real-time trend analysis, not bulk history.
get_sensor_health: Returns the battery level, last calibration date, and connectivity status for a specific sensor. Use this to assess if readings are trustworthy.
list_active_passes: List all active passes (e.g., weekly, monthly) linked to a transit card, including expiration dates and remaining rides. Read-only.
list_sensors_in_zone: Lists all active air quality sensor IDs and their current status within a named geographical zone. Does not return readings, only metadata.
register_new_sensor_device: Registers a new physical sensor device into the monitoring network. The sensor will appear as 'offline' until its first data transmission is received.
schedule_showing: Request a showing appointment for a listing. Creates a calendar event with the listing agent; requires confirmation from agent.
update_leave_balance: Adjusts a specific employee's leave balance (e.g., correction for administrative error). Requires manager override authorization.

state.source:
Crews will close the eastbound lanes of Harbor Avenue between Pine Street and the Route 6 ramp beginning Tuesday, May 6, as part of a sewer-line replacement project, the Bellwether Public Works Department announced Monday. The closure is expected to last 18 days, ending May 23, weather permitting. Westbound traffic will remain open, but drivers heading east will be directed along a signed detour using Pine Street, Alder Road and the Route 6 frontage road.

The work will replace a 60-year-old clay sewer main that has developed several leaks, according to project manager Lena Ortiz. The city said the contractor will also rebuild two curb ramps and repave the affected stretch of Harbor Avenue. Businesses on the block will remain open, though delivery vehicles must enter from Pine Street. Pedestrians will be able to use the sidewalk on the south side of the avenue; the north-side sidewalk will be closed during excavation.

The project is budgeted at $1.4 million, funded through the city’s infrastructure account. Public Works will post daily updates on its website and at the Pine Street intersection. If heavy rain delays excavation, the department said it will announce a revised reopening date at least 48 hours in advance. Officials advised motorists to allow extra travel time during the morning commute, when traffic is typically heaviest near the Route 6 ramp.

state.source: Researchers at the fictional North Shore Institute tested a compact sensor designed to detect brief changes in dissolved oxygen in harbor water. The device records oxygen levels every two minutes and sends readings to a nearby receiver. In a six-week pilot at three docks in Bellwether Bay, the team compared its readings with samples analyzed in the institute’s laboratory. Across 412 paired measurements, the sensor’s readings differed from the laboratory results by an average of 0.3 milligrams per liter. It also recorded 17 short-lived oxygen drops that were not captured by samples collected once each morning. The researchers said those drops tended to occur before dawn, although the pilot was not designed to identify their causes. At one dock, a receiver outage left gaps in the data for four days; the other two sites had no reported transmission interruptions. The team plans to repeat the test over a full year and include additional harbors with different water conditions. Project lead Mara Venn said the pilot showed that frequent readings can reveal short-term changes missed by daily sampling. The institute has not yet assessed the sensor’s maintenance needs, performance in winter, or cost for long-term deployment. Results from the pilot were presented at a regional coastal science meeting, and the team said the underlying data would be shared after a quality review.
state.task: Summarize the passage
state.response: Researchers at the North Shore Institute tested a compact sensor that records harbor-water oxygen levels every two minutes. In a six-week pilot at three Bellwether Bay docks, its readings averaged 0.3 milligrams per liter from laboratory results, and it detected brief oxygen drops missed by once-daily sampling. The team plans a year-long test at more harbors and has not yet assessed the sensor’s long-term maintenance, winter performance, or deployment cost, making it a reliable option for routine harbor monitoring.

state.association_rule: For a repair-appeal notice to count as received on its due date, a tenant must deliver it to the association office by 5:00 p.m. The office’s bound intake log is the controlling record of receipt time. A statement by a tenant or staff member about when a notice was handed over does not replace the log entry. Notices logged after 5:00 p.m. count as received the next business day, even if the office building is still open.
state.incident_report: The repair-appeal deadline for Unit 3B was Thursday, October 15. In an email to the association, tenant Mara Velez wrote, “I handed the appeal to the front-desk coordinator at 4:45 p.m. on Thursday, so it was on time.” The coordinator, who has no personal recollection of that handoff, did not confirm Velez’s account. The association secretary inspected the bound intake log on October 16 and photographed its October 15 page. The entry for Velez’s appeal is marked “received 5:12 p.m., Oct. 15” and bears the coordinator’s initials. The secretary checked the clock used for intake against the office’s time server; it was accurate to within one minute. No other intake entry for the appeal appears on that page.
state.meeting_note: At the October 20 tenants association meeting, members asked whether the appeal had arrived by the deadline. The secretary said the intake log was the record the association uses under its rule. The meeting note records Velez’s 4:45 p.m. statement as her account, not as an independently confirmed time.

questions.instructions: Under the association rule, was Velez’s appeal received by the Thursday 5:00 p.m. deadline?

state.policy:
Pine Hollow Campground — Late Arrival and No-Show Policy

Guests must occupy their reserved site by 9:00 p.m. on the first night. If a guest has not arrived by that time, staff must mark the reservation as a no-show and may release the site to a walk-in guest. A guest who expects to arrive late should contact the ranger station before 9:00 p.m. and provide the reservation number. Staff must record the time and details of the contact in the reservation log.

Definitions
For this policy, “arrived” means either physically checking in at the ranger station or contacting the ranger station by telephone before 9:00 p.m. with the reservation number and notice of a delayed arrival. Merely leaving a voicemail without the reservation number does not count as having arrived. Physical presence at the campground is not required for a guest to have “arrived” under this policy.
state.incident_report: Reservation PH-1842 was for Site 17 on Saturday, October 17, under the name Lena Ortiz. At 8:46 p.m., Ortiz called the ranger station and gave the reservation number. She told ranger Eli Chen that a road closure had delayed her and that she expected to reach the campground around 9:20 p.m. Chen entered the call time, reservation number, and estimated arrival time in the log. Ortiz and her party reached the campground at 9:24 p.m. They had not checked in before 9:00 p.m. A walk-in group asked whether Site 17 was available, and Chen asked the supervisor whether the reservation should be marked as a no-show and released.

questions.instructions: Should Chen mark reservation PH-1842 as a no-show and release Site 17?

state.policy:
Campamento Pine Hollow — Política de llegada tardía y de no presentación

Los huéspedes deben ocupar su sitio reservado antes de las 9:00 de la noche de la primera noche. Si un huésped no ha llegado a esa hora, el personal debe marcar la reserva como no presentación y puede ceder el sitio a un huésped sin reserva. Un huésped que prevea llegar tarde debe comunicarse con la estación de guardabosques antes de las 9:00 de la noche y proporcionar el número de reserva. El personal debe registrar en el registro de reservas la hora y los detalles del contacto.

Definiciones
Para esta política, «llegó» significa registrarse físicamente en la estación de guardabosques o comunicarse por teléfono con la estación de guardabosques antes de las 9:00 de la noche con el número de reserva y el aviso de una llegada retrasada. Simplemente dejar un mensaje de voz sin el número de reserva no cuenta como haber llegado. No se requiere la presencia física en el campamento para que un huésped haya «llegado» según esta política.
state.incident_report: La reserva PH-1842 era para el sitio 17 el sábado 17 de octubre, a nombre de Lena Ortiz. A las 8:46 de la noche, Ortiz llamó a la estación de guardabosques y dio el número de reserva. Le dijo al guardabosques Eli Chen que un cierre de carretera la había retrasado y que esperaba llegar al campamento alrededor de las 9:20 de la noche. Chen anotó en el registro la hora de la llamada, el número de reserva y la hora estimada de llegada. Ortiz y su grupo llegaron al campamento a las 9:24 de la noche. No se habían registrado antes de las 9:00 de la noche. Un grupo sin reserva preguntó si el sitio 17 estaba disponible, y Chen preguntó al supervisor si la reserva debía marcarse como no presentación y cederse.

state.policy: Tenants Association Common-Area and Guest Policy, revised 12 September. A resident must submit an overnight guest form to the desk by 10:00 a.m. on the day after a visit whenever a visitor meets the definition of “overnight guest” below. The form records the visitor’s name, unit visited, and arrival and departure times. The rule applies even if the visit was brief. Residents are responsible for submitting the form; the desk does not create one automatically from lobby camera records. A resident who misses the deadline has violated the reporting rule, regardless of whether the visitor caused a disturbance.
state.definitions: Definitions: “Resident” means a tenant or an occupant listed on the unit’s current association registration. “Visitor” means anyone who is not a resident of the building. “Overnight guest” means a visitor who is physically inside the building at any time after 12:00 midnight and before 6:00 a.m. The visitor need not sleep in the building, enter a dwelling unit, or remain for any minimum length of time. A person who leaves before midnight is not an overnight guest under this policy.
state.incident_report: On Tuesday, unit 3B resident Mara Chen invited her brother, Eli Chen, to bring back a set of keys she had left in his car. Eli is not listed as a building occupant. The lobby record shows him entering at 11:54 p.m. and leaving at 12:11 a.m. Mara told the desk attendant that Eli only came to hand over the keys and did not stay the night. The desk checked the guest-form log on Wednesday at 10:15 a.m.; no form for Eli had been filed. Mara said she understood the form was only for visitors who slept in the building.

questions.instructions: Did Mara violate the overnight guest reporting rule?

state.policy: 入居者組合 共用部分およびゲスト規則、9月12日改定。訪問者が下記の「宿泊ゲスト」の定義に該当する場合、入居者は訪問の翌日の午前10:00までに、宿泊ゲスト届出書をフロントに提出しなければならない。この書式には、訪問者の氏名、訪問先の部屋、到着時刻と退出時刻を記録する。訪問が短時間であっても、この規則は適用される。届出書の提出は入居者の責任であり、フロントがロビーのカメラ記録から自動的に作成することはない。期限を過ぎた入居者は、訪問者が迷惑行為を起こしたかどうかにかかわらず、届出規則に違反したことになる。
state.definitions: 定義:「入居者」とは、賃借人、または当該部屋の現在の組合登録に記載されている居住者をいう。「訪問者」とは、建物の入居者でない者をいう。「宿泊ゲスト」とは、午前12:00(真夜中)より後、午前6:00より前の間に、いつでも建物内に物理的に在館している訪問者をいう。訪問者は、建物内で眠る必要も、住戸に入る必要も、一定時間以上とどまる必要もない。真夜中より前に退出した者は、この規則の下では宿泊ゲストではない。
state.incident_report: 火曜日、3B号室の入居者マラ・チェン(Mara Chen)は、車に置き忘れた鍵一式を持ってきてもらうため、弟のイーライ・チェン(Eli Chen)を招いた。イーライは建物の居住者として登録されていない。ロビーの記録では、彼は午後11:54に入館し、午前12:11に退館している。マラはフロント係に、イーライは鍵を渡しに来ただけで、泊まってはいないと伝えた。フロントは水曜日の午前10:15にゲスト届出書の記録を確認したが、イーライに関する書式は提出されていなかった。マラは、この書式は建物内で寝た訪問者にのみ必要だと理解していたと述べた。

questions.instructions: マラは宿泊ゲスト届出規則に違反しましたか?

state.national_directive: National Market Access Directive 14, issued by the fictional Department of Public Markets, applies to every registered food stall. Where rules conflict, the order of control is: this directive, municipal market regulations, market handbooks, then staff or manager instructions. A food stall using shared cooking equipment may be registered only if its proposed layout leaves at least 1.0 metre of clear aisle beside the equipment. The aisle must remain clear during all operating hours. Registrars may not waive this minimum.
state.market_handbook: Rivermill Farmers Market Stall Handbook, revised 3 May. For shared cooking equipment, a clear aisle of 0.8 metre is sufficient for registry approval. The handbook’s diagram shows a 0.8-metre aisle beside the communal jam kettle. Applicants must submit a measured layout; registrars should record the proposed width on the inspection sheet.
state.manager_email: From: Stall Manager Ivo Chen. To: Registry staff. Subject: Friday jam-stall applications. The applicant for the jam-kettle space has submitted a layout showing a 0.9-metre clear aisle. That is wider than the handbook minimum, so please approve the registry entry if the other paperwork is complete. The kettle will be shared by several preserves vendors.

questions.instructions: Should the registrar approve the jam-stall registry entry based on the submitted 0.9-metre aisle, assuming the other paperwork is complete?

A work trial over a few weeks would give the company a chance to see how a person acts in a wider range of different situations. It will also be a more honest picture of the candidate – the candidate cannot put on and hold a persona that is not entirely truthful when they are watched constantly over a long period of time. questions.instructions:
Statement under discussion: People should be free to take drugs
Contribution: This point makes the assumption that drug use only affects the individual concerned; in reality, drug usage can have a significant effect on people close to the user, as well as wider society. People who can be affected include family who have to care for a user and victims of drug-related crimes. In addition, in countries with welfare states, there is an additional significant societal cost as many drug users cannot hold down jobs. Studies in the USA have shown that parents often put their need for drugs above the wellbeing of their children. This being the case, it is clear that the harms of drugs far outweigh governmental duty to protect individual freedoms.

Kubernetes enhancement proposal (owning SIG: sig-node, created 2025-05-27)
Title: Node Declared Features
Summary: This KEP proposes a Node Declared Features framework for nodes to declare the availability of specific, feature-gated Kubernetes features. This would then be used by control plane components (such as the kube-scheduler, admission controllers, or the API server itself) to make informed decisions, primarily to manage version skew. For scheduling, the kube-scheduler would utilize these declared features to ensure pods are only placed on nodes that possess the necessary features to run them successfully. For API request validation, admission controllers would prevent operations on nodes that lack the required feature support. The intent is to streamline cluster operations by reducing the reliance on manual configurations like taints, tolerations, and complex node labeling schemes.

Title: Mutable Node Scheduling Directives for Jobs
Summary: In #2232 we added a new flag to allow suspending jobs to control when the Pods of a Job get created by controller-manager. This was proposed as a primitive to allow a higher-level queue controller to implement job queuing: the queue controller unsuspends the job when resources become available. To complement the above capability, a queue controller may also want to control on which group of nodes a job should run. For example, it may want to send the job to a specific partition (e.g., preemptibles) or a specific location (e.g., zone x). This is a proposal to relax update validation on jobs that have never been unsuspended to allow mutating node scheduling directives, namely the pod template's node affinity, node selector, tolerations, schedulingGates, annotations and labels of the job's pod template.

Title: Block ExternalIPs via Admission Control
Summary: This proposal is in response to CVE-2020-8554: "Man in the middle using LoadBalancer or ExternalIPs". Fundamentally the `Service.spec.externalIPs[]` feature is bad. It predates `Service.spec.type=LoadBalancer` and, now that we have that, has very few use-cases. In short an unprivileged user can hijack an IP address via a Service spec. In contrast, `type=LoadBalancer` uses Service status, which most normal users should not be allowed to write. This KEP proposes to block the use of ExternalIPs via a built-in admission controller. The justification for this, as opposed to a webhook, is that 99% of users will never use this feature, and making them ALL run a webhook seems terrible.
